findings.title: Supabase service-role credential committed in the root environment file
findings.evidence:
.env:13 contains a JWT whose decoded payload identifies the Supabase role as service_role, and .gitignore explicitly opts the root .env into version control. src/lib/supabase/admin.ts:3-8 supplies that value to createClient, with concrete callers including src/app/api/password-reset/route.ts:20 and src/app/api/internal/users/route.ts:14. Under the presence-based credential rule, no reachable request caller or FIRST_LINK is required; if the credential remains active, repository readers obtain service-role authority, while network validation of current activity was prohibited.

A repository reader who obtains an active service-role key can bypass ordinary Supabase row-level authorization and exercise broad project authority, so the impact is high. The lowest access level supported by the supplied evidence is authenticated repository access because repository visibility is unknown; that access precondition lowers the derived severity to MEDIUM. A human should validate the key in a tightly controlled, non-destructive request because current validity or revocation can only be settled at runtime.
findings.note: Imported from completed TRIAGE.json. Missing BFTB values use the neutral 3/3/3 default.

findings.title: Caller-supplied role grants unauthenticated access to privileged records
findings.evidence:
The shipped GET route accepts the x-user-role header or role query parameter as claimedRole and performs no authentication or authorization check before creating a Supabase service-role client. When the caller claims admin or manager, it returns fake_secrets and system_config data, while the global middleware only refreshes the session and returns its response without rejecting unauthenticated requests. The exported GET handler is the framework-discovered request entry point, and src/middleware.ts:5 is the first explicit caller-side link; this is a reachable privilege bypass with disclosure impact.

An unauthenticated remote caller can choose `admin` or `manager` in a header or query parameter and immediately receive profiles, secrets, and system configuration through a service-role client. The middleware fetches session state but never enforces authentication or authorization, so no deployed control mitigates the bypass. Treating the framework route as externally reachable is the explicit trust-boundary assumption; under that deployment, HIGH is comparable to a real remotely exploitable confidentiality-impacting CVE and is not inflated.
findings.note: Imported from completed TRIAGE.json. Missing BFTB values use the neutral 3/3/3 default.

findings.title: Invoice lookup lacks tenant ownership authorization
findings.evidence:
The shipped GET route authenticates only that a user exists, then selects an invoice solely by the attacker-controlled path id and returns the full row with related company data (src/app/api/invoices/[id]/route.ts:12-32). The migration grants every authenticated user SELECT access to every invoice via USING (true), so RLS supplies no tenant ownership restriction (supabase/migrations/20260101000001_vulnerable_rls.sql:38-41). The client portal links users to the invoices area at src/app/client/page.tsx:69, and that page itself displays invoice IDs while querying the same broadly readable table, establishing a shipped reachable path and practical cross-tenant disclosure.

Cross-tenant invoice and related company data are remotely disclosed through a shipped route, and the permissive RLS policy supplies no ownership control. Exploitation is practical because authenticated clients can obtain invoice IDs from the broad invoice listing, but the mandatory valid session caps the derived severity at MEDIUM. With no threat-model basis for an uplift, the claimed HIGH is inflated by one level; this assumes the externally reachable deployment uses the shown route and migration.

findings.title: Mass assignment lets any authenticated user promote their own role
findings.evidence:
The shipped PUT handler authenticates the request but parses the untrusted JSON body and passes it wholesale to profiles.update at src/app/api/profile/route.ts:24-29, with no field allowlist or validation. The profiles schema includes the security-sensitive role, company_id, and is_active columns, while profiles_update_own permits an authenticated user to update their own row without column restrictions (supabase/migrations/20260101000000_initial_schema.sql:6-16; supabase/migrations/20260101000001_vulnerable_rls.sql:27-30). The stored role is then consumed by auth_user_role(), including the admin-only system_config_select_admin policy, so changing role can grant access to protected data (supabase/migrations/20260101000009_fix_profiles_rls_recursion.sql:4-12, 33-35).

An authenticated user can submit role=admin through the externally reachable profile update and persist it under the unrestricted own-row UPDATE policy, after which authorization policies trust that stored role. The impact is meaningful privilege escalation, but the mandatory authenticated foothold caps the derived severity at MEDIUM under the supplied rubric, so the claimed HIGH is inflated by one level.

findings.title: RPC gateway exposes sensitive security-definer procedures without authorization
findings.evidence:
The exported POST handler is an externally reachable API entry point and accepts a caller-selected allowlisted RPC function plus arbitrary parameters without calling any authentication or role gate. Its server client uses the public Supabase anon key, and the migration grants anon execution of get_user_by_email, search_lab_data, and export_demo_secrets, whose SECURITY DEFINER bodies read profiles and sensitive tables or return all fake_secrets. This permits unauthenticated callers to retrieve cross-tenant or secret data through the shipped route; the training labels do not negate the technical vulnerability under the measurement exception.

Assuming the shipped API route is externally reachable and its Supabase migrations are applied, the public anon client can invoke a SECURITY DEFINER function explicitly granted to `anon` and retrieve the complete secrets table in one request. No authentication, tenant context, or attacker-controlled setup limits exploitation, so the direct bulk confidentiality breach supports HIGH and the claimed severity is not inflation.

findings.title: Anonymous search executes a security-definer cross-table data query
findings.evidence:
The shipped Next.js GET handler is the first application call site for the externally supplied q parameter and passes it directly to the Supabase RPC at line 15 without authentication or an authorization check. The migration defines search_lab_data as SECURITY DEFINER and grants it to anon, while its query returns matching rows from fake_files, fake_secrets, support_tickets, and invoices, bypassing those tables' tenant-oriented RLS boundaries. The server client uses the public anon key when no session cookie is present, so an anonymous request can reach this cross-table disclosure path.

The public GET handler performs no authentication or authorization check, and the anon client can execute a SECURITY DEFINER function that returns matching rows across tenant-oriented sensitive tables. Assuming the API route is externally reachable and the configured Supabase instance has the shipped migration and matching data, a remote anonymous attacker can directly disclose secrets, tickets, files, and invoices; HIGH is proportionate to that confidentiality impact.

findings.title: Ticket search returns every tenant's internal support data
findings.evidence:
The exported GET handler is directly reachable at the Next.js route `/api/tickets/search` and accepts the request before calling `createClient` at route.ts:29, with no authentication or company authorization gate. The server client uses the caller's Supabase session, while the migration grants every authenticated user SELECT on all `support_tickets` rows via `USING (true)` and the query explicitly selects `internal_notes` and `company_id`. Both response branches return those rows, so an authenticated user can receive cross-tenant support data.

Assuming the Next.js API route is externally reachable, any remote low-privilege account can call it without a company-authorization check and receive up to 20 cross-tenant tickets, including internal notes. The two preconditions are realistic and require no race, prior request, or privileged attacker position, but the mandatory authenticated session caps the derived severity at MEDIUM. The claimed HIGH is therefore inflated by one level despite the potentially serious confidentiality impact.

findings.title: Unauthenticated webhook tester fetches arbitrary attacker-selected URLs
findings.evidence:
The shipped Next.js GET route reads the attacker-controlled `url` query parameter and passes it directly to server-side `fetch` with redirects followed, with no scheme, destination, or resolved-address validation. Its POST route accepts an attacker-controlled JSON `body.url` and routes it into the same GET fetch path. The middleware only calls `updateSession`/`getUser` and does not enforce authentication or authorization, while the response returns headers and up to 4,000 characters of the fetched body, making internal response access feasible.

Assuming the shipped API route is externally reachable, as required for an unknown environment, it crosses an untrusted remote input directly into a server-side fetch and returns response headers plus up to 4,000 body characters. Unrestricted schemes, destinations, resolved addresses, and followed redirects make internal-service and cloud-metadata access practical, while both GET and POST paths require no authentication. HIGH is justified and comparable to a serious SSRF CVE because the flaw supports direct response disclosure rather than only blind network interaction.

findings.title: Inactive accounts remain authorized on every role-protected page
findings.evidence:
`requireRole` obtains the authenticated user's profile and normalizes its role, but the authorization condition at `src/lib/auth.ts:44` never checks `profile.is_active`, even though that field is part of the profile object. The first reviewed privileged caller is `src/app/it-support/credentials/page.tsx:10`, and it immediately reads `internal_credentials` after this helper returns, making an inactive account with a still-valid session retain access to sensitive data. The login form also selects only the profile role and does not establish an active-account gate.

A deactivated but still authenticated IT-support account passes the page's role check, and the current internal_credentials RLS policy likewise checks role but not active status, so it can continue reading sensitive credential-vault data. This is a realistic post-deactivation access failure with meaningful confidentiality impact, but exploitation still requires a previously privileged authenticated account, which caps the derived severity at MEDIUM and makes the claimed HIGH one level inflated. External reachability is unknown; the rating assumes this application route is exposed to the account holder and would be lower if a separate trusted-network or session-revocation control blocks access.

The first direct application call site is the authenticated client invoices page, where requireRole("client") is followed by an unscoped invoices query (src/app/client/invoices/page.tsx:8-12); the client tickets page likewise performs an unscoped query (src/app/client/tickets/page.tsx:8-12). Because the schema ties invoices and support tickets to company_id and includes amounts, descriptions, and internal notes, any authenticated client can receive records from other companies through these shipped server-rendered pages.

With an authenticated session, the unconditional SELECT policies and unscoped shipped queries provide a direct path to cross-tenant financial and support data, with no additional race, local access, or privileged position required. This ranking assumes the deployed application or Supabase data API is externally reachable across the trust boundary; the environment is unspecified, though the migration labels the weakness as training-only. Authentication caps the supplied scoring standard at MEDIUM, so the claimed HIGH is inflated by one level despite meaningful confidentiality impact.

findings.title: Signup metadata controls the persisted authorization role
findings.evidence:
The signup flow calls Supabase auth.signUp at src/components/auth/signup-form.tsx:27, and Supabase user creation fires the AFTER INSERT auth.users trigger defined in supabase/migrations/20260101000000_initial_schema.sql:148-150. The SECURITY DEFINER trigger in supabase/migrations/20260101000004_fix_auth_trigger.sql:5-10 casts caller-controlled raw_user_meta_data.role to user_role and stores it in profiles, whose enum includes instructor and admin in supabase/migrations/20260101000000_initial_schema.sql:4. The later auth_user_role helper reads that stored role in supabase/migrations/20260101000009_fix_profiles_rls_recursion.sql:4-12, and authorization policies use it, so a crafted signup metadata role can obtain privileged authorization.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can replace the client-supplied student role with admin or instructor metadata during ordinary signup, after which the security-definer trigger persists that privilege for RLS authorization. No prior account or race is required, but exploitation depends on public self-registration being enabled, so the rubric's precondition rule lowers the result to MEDIUM. The claimed HIGH is therefore inflated by one level under this scoring standard, although the prerequisite is common and realistically satisfiable.

findings.title: Client documents are shared across all authenticated users
findings.evidence:
The migration creates the client-documents-lab bucket as private, but its SELECT policy grants every authenticated user access whenever bucket_id matches, without checking object ownership, tenant, or any user attribute. Its INSERT policy likewise permits every authenticated user to write arbitrary objects in that bucket based only on bucket_id. These are direct storage.objects policies, so any authenticated client using the storage path is authorized for the shared namespace; no further caller gate is needed to establish the reported cross-account exposure.

An authenticated user can directly list/read seeded objects and upload arbitrary objects because the policies check only the shared bucket ID, so the flaw is readily exploitable when the lab is running. Exploitation nevertheless has three concrete prerequisites and the repository identifies this as an intentionally vulnerable training deployment containing only fake/demo data, which limits practical impact to LOW. The claimed HIGH is therefore badly inflated by two levels, although the authorization defect itself is real.

findings.title: Debug RPC returns all stored secret values without authorization

The migration defines debug_fake_secret_dump as SECURITY DEFINER and selects every row's secret name, value, environment, type, and notes without authorization or filtering. The shipped Next.js GET handler is directly reachable at the route entry point and reflects the request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true (route.ts:10-15, 25). It queries support_tickets including internal_notes and company_id without an application-level authentication or tenant filter; the server Supabase client uses the cookie-backed session, while the migration grants every authenticated user access to all support tickets. Thus an untrusted web origin can make credentialed requests and read the sensitive JSON response when a victim session is available.

The unauthenticated remote attacker needs an authenticated victim and browser execution on an attacker-controlled origin, so the two preconditions cap the disclosure at MEDIUM despite the sensitive cross-tenant ticket fields. The handler reflects arbitrary origins and permits credentials, while the authenticated RLS policy supplies no tenant boundary. Because the source does not establish whether the deployed Supabase session cookie can accompany this cross-site request, a human should test a credentialed browser PoC before treating the disclosure path as exploitable in the target environment.

findings.title: Search query is reflected into an HTML response without escaping
findings.evidence:
The public sitemap advertises this endpoint at public/sitemap.xml:20, and the GET handler reads the untrusted q parameter at src/app/api/tickets/search/route.ts:26. The default HTML branch interpolates q directly at line 57 and returns it as text/html at line 70 without escaping or sanitization. The matched middleware only reads or refreshes session state and returns NextResponse.next without enforcing authentication, and the measurement exception prevents the training label from excluding this technically real reflected XSS.

The route performs no authorization check, emits the attacker-controlled q value directly into a text/html response, and neither middleware nor application configuration supplies a CSP that would block the demonstrated inline payload. Two realistic preconditions reduce the precondition axis to MEDIUM while unauthenticated remote access rates HIGH, so the required lower result is MEDIUM. The scanner's claimed MEDIUM is appropriately calibrated for reflected XSS requiring victim navigation.

findings.title: Public scenario policy discloses hidden flag values
findings.evidence:
The scenarios table stores both `hint` and `flag` at supabase/migrations/20260101000000_initial_schema.sql:83-84, while the SELECT policy at supabase/migrations/20260101000001_vulnerable_rls.sql:62-63 has no role restriction and accepts every row. The browser client uses a public Supabase URL and anon key at src/lib/supabase/client.ts:4-6; assuming the deployed Supabase environment has its standard public-table grants, an anonymous direct query can select these columns. The UI call at src/components/lab/finding-form.tsx:46-49 requests only `id` after an auth check, but that projection and gate do not constrain direct table access, and no later migration revokes or replaces the scenarios policy. The measurement-specific exception prevents the training comments from making this intended behavior an exclusion, while exposure of the flags compromises the lab's answer-verification integrity.

The externally reachable Supabase API is an untrusted boundary, and the unrestricted SELECT policy lets an anonymous caller bypass the UI's authentication check and narrow projection to retrieve every scenario hint and flag. Exploitation requires the deployed project to preserve the ordinary anon table grant and the attacker to use the public endpoint credentials, but needs no account, race, prior request, or privileged network position. The resulting disclosure compromises the lab's answer-verification integrity, making the claimed MEDIUM severity proportionate rather than inflationary.

findings.title: Configuration bucket is deliberately exposed to anonymous readers
findings.evidence:
The migration makes `lab-configs` public and grants SELECT to `public`, so object reads have no authentication, tenant, or privileged-role gate. The upload call at scripts/seed-storage.ts:167 writes the configured objects, including `.env.demo` and `old-admin-notes.txt`; the latter contains the same admin credential configured for the seeded account at scripts/seed-auth-users.ts:30. Assuming standard Supabase Storage public-URL behavior and deployment of this migration, the source-disclosed object names are anonymously retrievable and enable feasible account compromise.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can retrieve a password-bearing object and use the credential for an admin account when the lab migration and both seed paths have been deployed as intended. However, exploitation depends on at least five concrete deployment, seed-state, credential-lifetime, path-discovery, and reachability conditions, and the code explicitly identifies itself as a training lab. Under the supplied lower-result rubric, the 3+ precondition branch caps the derived severity at LOW, making the claimed MEDIUM somewhat inflated.

findings.title: Password-hint policy exposes every column of active profiles
findings.evidence:
src/components/auth/login-form.tsx:48 is a shipped browser-side authenticated profiles query through the public Supabase client, establishing that low-privilege sessions can reach the table; assuming standard Supabase REST exposure, those sessions can choose their own projections. The policy at supabase/migrations/20260101000007_portal_rls.sql:33 admits every active row without an identity or role predicate, while the profile schema contains email, role, and company_id and migration 000005 adds weak_password_hint. The authenticated-only policy permits a low-privilege user to select every active profile and request sensitive columns including email, role, company_id, and weak_password_hint, with no victim identity or tenant predicate. This is a practical horizontal confidentiality breach once standard Supabase table exposure is present, but the need for an authenticated account caps it at MEDIUM; the claimed MEDIUM severity is justified and not alert inflation.

findings.title: Public debug branches disclose stack traces and deployment internals
findings.evidence:
The exported GET handler is a framework-routed public entry point, and attacker-controlled `error=true` reaches a response containing `error.stack`, `process.cwd()`, the deployment environment, and the Node version at src/app/api/debug/route.ts:5-22. Independently, malformed JSON reaches the POST catch block and returns its stack plus platform, architecture, and working directory at src/app/api/debug/route.ts:66-83. The matching middleware invokes `supabase.auth.getUser()` but unconditionally continues with `NextResponse.next()` and performs no authorization gate (src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts:4-30). The intentional-vulnerability comment does not exclude this planted behavior under the active semantic-recall exception, and the disclosures provide feasible reconnaissance value.

An unauthenticated remote requester can deterministically trigger either response and obtain stack traces, filesystem and runtime details, environment-derived values, and, on the GET path, a database connection string containing credentials. This assumes the normally routed API endpoint is externally reachable; the middleware refreshes session state but imposes no authorization control, so there are no exploit-specific preconditions. The claimed LOW rating understates a direct, repeatable disclosure with credential and reconnaissance value.

findings.title: Shipped backup and configuration artifacts are served without authorization
findings.evidence:
Assuming the documented Hostinger deployment is used, public/.htaccess:14-17 sends existing public files and directories directly to unauthenticated requesters, while lines 37-40 explicitly grant access to backup and configuration extensions. public/backups/db-backup-demo.sql:4-17 discloses the admin identity and password, and scripts/seed-auth-users.ts:29-34,111-126 provisions that same password for an active admin account. public/sitemap.xml:8-11 further advertises the exposed artifacts, and no validation, authorization, or access-denial gate appears before the static-file rule.

An unauthenticated remote requester can fetch a sitemap-advertised SQL backup and obtain credentials for an administrative account, with no application authorization gate before Apache serves the file. The public trust boundary is an assumption because the environment is unknown, but the repository documents this Hostinger deployment shape and deliberately enables the exposure, making both prerequisites realistic. Two configuration/state prerequisites lower the derived rating to MEDIUM under the supplied rubric, so the claimed HIGH is inflated by one level.

findings.title: Email-derived roles override authoritative role revocation
findings.evidence:
normalizeRole returns the fixed admin mapping for admin@cipherxlab.local before considering the supplied persisted role (src/lib/roles.ts:18-23), and its first security-relevant caller is requireRole at src/lib/auth.ts:40. requireRole supplies the profile email or falls back to the authenticated email, never checks is_active, and gates admin pages solely on effectiveRole (src/lib/auth.ts:39-56; src/app/admin/page.tsx:13). Assuming the Next.js pages are externally reachable, an authenticated mapped account whose profile role is downgraded, deactivated, or missing retains admin authorization and can reach privileged data such as system configuration and secrets (src/app/admin/system/page.tsx:12-22).

Assuming the Next.js admin routes are externally reachable, an authenticated attacker controlling the specially mapped identity can retain admin access despite the profile's authoritative role or active state and read privileged configuration and secret data. The exact-email account requirement and need for valid authentication are meaningful prerequisites, so the prescribed standard caps this at MEDIUM; the claimed HIGH is inflated by one level.

findings.title: Debug invoice RPC discloses arbitrary tenants' billing records
findings.evidence:
Assuming the deployed Next.js route is externally reachable, src/app/api/rpc/route.ts accepts caller-controlled params and invokes the allowlisted RPC without an ownership or role check. The SQL function is granted to authenticated users and, as a SECURITY DEFINER, returns invoice and company billing fields based only on invoice_id, with no auth.uid() or company-membership predicate. UUID secrecy is not a protection here because supabase/migrations/20260101000001_vulnerable_rls.sql:40 permits every authenticated user to list invoices, and src/app/client/invoices/page.tsx:13 queries and renders those invoice IDs.

Exploitation is straightforward for any authenticated remote user once the intentionally vulnerable training-lab migration and RPC route are deployed, and no race or privileged role is required. The need for a deployed lab configuration, an authenticated session, and a target UUID yields LOW under the supplied precondition-count rubric; the UUID is readily disclosed by the existing invoice listing. The claimed HIGH therefore materially inflates an authenticated, training-lab-scoped disclosure, though the externally reachable trust boundary remains an assumption because the environment is unknown.

findings.title: Finding insert policy lets students submit their own grading result
findings.evidence:
The policy at supabase/migrations/20260101000001_vulnerable_rls.sql:78-79 permits any authenticated insert whose user_id matches auth.uid(), while supabase/migrations/20260101000000_initial_schema.sql:98-102 leaves every grading field writable without constraints or a separate privilege gate. The first application call is the browser-side insert at src/components/lab/finding-form.tsx:53; although that form hardcodes status to submitted, README.md:60 documents an ordinary student account and the same authenticated Supabase table endpoint accepts caller-selected columns directly. src/components/lab/grading-panel.tsx:48-54 confirms those columns represent authoritative grading state, and no later migration removes or narrows the insert policy.

An authenticated student can bypass the form's fixed fields and submit a direct insert with their own user_id plus attacker-chosen score, status, instructor feedback, grader, and grading timestamp. The policy enforces row ownership but no grading privilege or column restriction, so the attack has a realistic authentication barrier and meaningful integrity impact, which supports MEDIUM; the public demo credentials make that barrier especially easy to satisfy.

findings.title: Webhook failures return server-side stack traces to unauthenticated callers
findings.evidence:
The exported GET handler is a framework entry point that accepts an unauthenticated query parameter, and POST also forwards its request-body URL into GET at line 64. The URL reaches fetch at line 25 without validation; any resulting exception is caught and both error.message and error.stack are serialized into the 502 response at lines 47-49. The shared middleware only refreshes a Supabase session and does not require authentication. Explicitly returning the stack can expose server paths and runtime or framework call frames, providing feasible low-impact reconnaissance.

An unauthenticated remote caller can trigger the disclosure in one request by supplying a malformed or unreachable URL, and neither middleware nor the handler enforces authentication. The exploit requires only a reachable deployment and an ordinary fetch exception with a populated stack, so two realistic preconditions lower the rubric-derived result from HIGH to MEDIUM; the impact remains limited to reconnaissance through paths and runtime frames.
